danish.title: Anden bog (1805) — Kapitel 12
paragraphs: Ved levéen stod fyrst Andrej blandt de østrigske officerer, som man havde sagt ham, og kejser Franz nøjedes med at se ham fast i ansigtet og nikke med sit lange hoved. Men efter levéen meddelte den adjudant, han havde set dagen før, ham med ceremoniel høflighed, at kejseren ønskede at give ham audiens. Kejser Franz modtog ham stående midt i værelset. Inden samtalen begyndte, slog det fyrst Andrej, at kejseren virkede forvirret og rødmede, som om han ikke vidste, hvad han skulle sige.
"Sig mig, hvornår begyndte slaget?" spurgte han hurtigt.

Fyrst Andrej svarede. Derefter fulgte andre lige så enkle spørgsmål: "Havde Kutuzov det godt? Hvornår havde han forladt Krems?" og så videre. Kejseren talte, som om hans eneste mål var at stille et bestemt antal spørgsmål — svarene interesserede ham tydeligvis ikke.
"Hvad tid begyndte slaget?" spurgte kejseren.

"Jeg kan ikke oplyse Deres Majestæt, præcis hvad tid slaget begyndte ved fronten, men ved Dürrenstein, hvor jeg befandt mig, begyndte vores angreb efter klokken fem om eftermiddagen," svarede Bolkonskij, der blev mere livlig og forventede, at han ville få lejlighed til at give en pålidelig beretning, som han havde klar i hovedet, om alt, hvad han vidste og havde set. Men kejseren smilede og afbrød ham.
"Hvor mange mil?"
"Fra hvor til hvor, Deres Majestæt?"
"Fra Dürrenstein til Krems."
"Tre og en halv mil, Deres Majestæt."
"Har franskmændene forladt venstre bred?"
"Ifølge spejderne krydsede de sidste på tømmerflåder i løbet af natten."
"Er der tilstrækkelig fourage i Krems?"
"Fourageforsyningen er ikke blevet leveret i det omfang ..."
Kejseren afbrød ham.
"Hvad tid faldt general Schmidt?"
"Klokken syv, tror jeg."
"Klokken syv? Det er meget sørgeligt, meget sørgeligt!"

Kejseren takkede fyrst Andrej og bukkede. Fyrst Andrej trak sig tilbage og blev straks omringet af hoffolk fra alle sider. Overalt mødte han venlige blikke og hørte venlige ord. Gårsdagens adjudant bebrejdede ham, at han ikke var blevet på paladset, og tilbød ham sit eget hus. Krigsministeren kom hen og lykønskede ham med Maria Theresia-ordenen af tredje grad, som kejseren tildelte ham. Kejserindens kammerherre indbød ham til at møde Hendes Majestæt. Ærkehertuginiden ønskede ligeledes at se ham. Han vidste ikke, hvem han skulle svare, og samlede i nogle sekunder sine tanker. Derpå tog den russiske ambassadør ham i skulderen, førte ham hen til vinduet og begyndte at tale med ham.

I modsætning til Bilibins forudsigelse blev nyheden, han bragte, modtaget med glæde. En takkegudstjeneste blev anordnet, Kutuzov blev tildelt Maria Theresia-ordenens Storkors, og hele hæren modtog belønninger. Bolkonskij blev inviteret overalt og måtte tilbringe hele formiddagen med at aflægge besøg hos de vigtigste østrigske honoratiores. Mellem fire og fem om eftermiddagen, efter at have aflagt alle sine besøg, vendte han tilbage til Bilibins hus, mens han overlagde et brev til sin far om slaget og sit ophold i Brünn. Ved indgangen fandt han et køretøj, halvt fyldt med bagage. Franz, Bilibins tjener, stod og slæbte en kuffert med besvær ud ad hoveddøren.
Inden han vendte tilbage til Bilibin, havde fyrst Andrej været i en boghandel for at forsyne sig med bøger til felttoget og havde tilbragt nogen tid i butikken.
"Hvad er der på færde?" spurgte han.
"Åh, Deres Eksellence!" sagde Franz, der med besvær rullede kufferten ind i vognen, "vi skal videre endnu længere. Slyngelen er igen i hælene på os!"
"Hvad? Hvad siger du?" spurgte fyrst Andrej.
Bilibin kom ud for at møde ham. Hans sædvanligvis rolige ansigt viste ophidselse.
"Nå! Indrøm, at det her er herligt," sagde han. "Den sag med Tabor-broen i Wien ... De er kommet over uden at løsne et skud!"
Fyrst Andrej forstod ikke.
"Men hvor kommer du fra, siden du ikke ved, hvad enhver droschkekusk i byen ved?"
"Jeg kommer fra ærkehertuginden. Der hørte jeg ingenting."
"Og du så ikke, at alle pakker sammen?"
"Det gjorde jeg ikke ... Hvad handler det hele om?" spurgte fyrst Andrej utålmodigt.
"Hvad det handler om? Franskmændene er gået over den bro, Auersperg forsvarede, og broen blev ikke sprængt: så nu er Murat på vej ad landevejen til Brünn og er her om en dag eller to."
"Hvad? Her? Men hvorfor sprængte de ikke broen, når den var mineret?"
"Det spørger jeg dig om. Ingen, ikke engang Bonaparte, ved hvorfor."
Bolkonskij trak på skuldrene.
"Men hvis broen er taget, er hæren også tabt? Den vil blive afskåret," sagde han.

"Netop," svarede Bilibin. "Hør nu! Franskmændene rykkede ind i Wien, som jeg fortalte dig. Godt. Næste dag, som var i går, stiger de herrer, messieurs les maréchaux — Murat, Lannes og Belliard — til hest og rider hen til broen. (Bemærk, at alle tre er gasconiere.) 'Mine herrer,' siger den ene, 'I ved, at Tabor-broen er mineret og dobbelt mineret, og at der er truende befæstninger ved brohovederne, og at en hær på femten tusind mand har ordre til at sprænge broen og ikke lade os komme over? Men det ville behage vor kejser Napoleon, hvis vi tog denne bro, så lad os tre gå og tage den!' 'Ja, lad os det!' siger de andre. Og af sted gik de og tog broen, krydsede den, og nu er de med hele deres hær på denne side af Donau og marcherer mod os, mod dig og dine forbindelseslinjer."
"Marskalerne."
"Hold op med at spøge," sagde fyrst Andrej sørgeligt og alvorligt. Denne nyhed bedrøvede ham, og dog var han tilfreds.

Så snart han hørte, at den russiske hær var i en så håbløs situation, slog det ham, at det var ham, der var bestemt til at føre den ud af den; at her var det Toulon, der ville løfte ham fra de ukendte officerers rækker og åbne den første vej til berømmelse! Mens han lyttede til Bilibin, forestillede han sig allerede, hvordan han ved ankomsten til hæren ville fremlægge et forslag ved krigsrådet, der ville være det eneste, som kunne redde hæren, og hvordan han alene ville blive betroet udførelsen af planen.
"Hold op med at spøge," sagde han.

"Jeg spøger ikke," fortsatte Bilibin. "Intet er mere sandt eller mere sørgeligt. Disse herrer rider alene hen på broen og vifter med hvide lommetørklæder; de forsikrer den vagthavende officer, at de, marskalerne, er på vej til at forhandle med fyrst Auersperg. Han lukker dem ind på brohovedets befæstning. De spinner ham en masse gasconader og fortæller, at krigen er forbi, at kejser Franz aftaler et møde med Bonaparte, at de gerne vil se fyrst Auersperg, og så videre. Officeren sender bud efter Auersperg; disse herrer omfavner officererne, slår vittigheder af, sætter sig på kanonerne, og imens sniger en fransk bataljon sig ubemærket hen til broen, kaster brandmaterialet i vandet og nærmer sig brohovedets befæstning. Endelig dukker generalløjtnanten op, vores kære fyrst Auersperg von Mautern i egen person. 'Kære fjende! Blomsten af den østrigske hær, den tyrkiske krigs helt! Fjendtlighederne er forbi, vi kan trykke hinanden i hånden ... Kejser Napoleon brænder af utålmodighed efter at lære fyrst Auersperg at kende.' Kort sagt, disse herrer — virkelig gasconiere — forblinder ham med smukke ord i en sådan grad, og han er så smigret over det hurtigt etablerede venskab med de franske marskaller og så blændet af synet af Murats kappe og strudsfjer, qu'il n'y voit que du feu, et oublie celui qu'il devait faire faire sur l'ennemi! (at han ikke ser andet end ild og glemmer den ild, han burde have ladet rette mod fjenden!)" Trods sin livlige tale glemte Bilibin ikke at holde en pause efter dette bonmot for at give det behørig påskønnelse. "Den franske bataljon styrter mod brohovedets befæstning, nagler kanonerne, og broen er taget! Men det allerbedste," fortsatte han, idet hans ophidselse lagde sig under den dejlige interesse i hans egen beretning, "er, at sergenten, der stod for den kanon, som skulle give signalet til at tænde minerne og sprænge broen, denne sergent, der ser de franske tropper storme ind på broen, er ved at fyre af, men Lannes holder hans hånd tilbage. Sergenten, der tydeligvis er klogere end sin general, går hen til Auersperg og siger: 'Fyrste, De bliver narret, her er franskmændene!' Murat ser, at alt er tabt, hvis sergenten får lov at tale, og vender sig med foregivet forbløffelse mod Auersperg (han er ægte gasconiér) og siger: 'Jeg genkender ikke den verdensberømte østrigske disciplin, når De tillader en underordnet at tiltale Dem på den måde!' Det var et genistreg. Fyrst Auersperg føler sin værdighed krænket og beordrer sergenten arresteret. Indrøm, at denne affære med Tabor-broen er herlig! Det er hverken direkte dumhed eller direkte skurkeri ..."
"Brohovedets befæstning."
"At deres ild blænder ham, og han glemmer den ild, han burde have rettet mod fjenden."
"Det er måske forræderi," sagde fyrst Andrej, der levende forestillede sig de grå kapper, sårene, krudtrøgen, skydningen og den hæder, der ventede ham.

"Heller ikke det. Det stiller hoffet i et for dårligt lys," svarede Bilibin. "Det er hverken forræderi, skurkeri eller dumhed; det er ligesom ved Ulm ... det er ..." — han syntes at lede efter det rigtige udtryk. "C'est ... c'est du Mack. Nous sommes mackés. (Det er ... det er noget à la Mack. Vi er blevet macket."" Han følte, at han havde produceret et godt bonmot, et nyt, der ville blive gentaget. Hans hidtil rynkede pande blev glat som tegn på tilfredshed, og med et let smil begyndte han at betragte sine negle.
"Hvor skal du hen?" sagde han pludselig til fyrst Andrej, der var rejst sig og gik mod sit værelse.
"Jeg rejser."
"Hvorhen?"
"Til hæren."
"Men du ville jo blive to dage endnu?"
"Men nu tager jeg af sted med det samme."
Og fyrst Andrej gik, efter at have givet anvisninger om sin afrejse, ind i sit værelse.
"Ved du hvad, mon cher," sagde Bilibin og fulgte efter ham, "jeg har tænkt over din situation. Hvorfor rejser du?"
Og til bevis for sin overbevisnings endegyldighed forsvandt alle rynkerne fra hans ansigt.
Fyrst Andrej kiggede spørgende på ham og svarede ikke.
"Hvorfor rejser du? Jeg ved, du mener, det er din pligt at galoppere tilbage til hæren, nu da den er i fare. Det forstår jeg. Mon cher, det er heltemod!"
"Slet ikke," sagde fyrst Andrej.

"Men som filosof bør du være konsekvent; betragt sagen fra den anden side, og du vil se, at din pligt tværtimod er at tage vare på dig selv. Overlad det til dem, der ikke duer til andet mere ... Du har ikke fået ordre til at vende tilbage og er ikke blevet afskediget herfra; altså kan du blive og følge med os, hvorhen vores uheld end fører os. De siger, vi tager til Olmütz, og Olmütz er en ganske pæn by. Du og jeg rejser behageligt i min kaleche."
"Hold op med at spøge, Bilibin," udbrød Bolkonskij.

"Jeg taler helt oprigtigt som en ven! Tænk dig om! Hvor og hvorfor skal du rejse, når du kan blive her? En af to ting venter dig" — og huden over hans venstre tinding rynkede sig — "enten når du ikke dit regiment, før freden er sluttet, eller du deler nederlag og vanære med hele Kutuzovs hær."
Og Bilibin glattede sin tinding i følelsen af, at dilemmaet var uløseligt.
"Det kan jeg ikke diskutere," svarede fyrst Andrej koldt, men tænkte: "Jeg tager af sted for at redde hæren."
"Min kære ven, du er en helt!" sagde Bilibin.

english.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: At the levee, Prince Andrew stood among the Austrian officers as instructed, and Emperor Francis merely stared fixedly at his face and gave a slight nod with his long head. But after it was over, the adjutant he'd seen the day before ceremoniously informed Bolkónski that the Emperor wished to grant him an audience. Emperor Francis received him standing in the middle of the room. Before the conversation began, Prince Andrew was struck by the fact that the Emperor seemed flustered and kept blushing, as if he didn't know what to say.
"Tell me, when did the battle begin?" he asked hastily.

Prince Andrew answered. Then came more questions, equally straightforward: "Was Kutúzov in good health? When had he left Krems?" The Emperor spoke as though his only goal were to get through a set number of questions—the answers, quite obviously, didn't interest him.
"At what time did the battle begin?" the Emperor asked.

"I cannot inform Your Majesty at what time the battle began at the front lines, but at Dürrenstein, where I was stationed, our attack began after five in the afternoon," replied Bolkónski, growing more animated and expecting he might finally have the chance to give a reliable account—which he had prepared in his mind—of all he knew and had seen. But the Emperor smiled and cut him off.
"How many miles?"
"From where to where, Your Majesty?"
"From Dürrenstein to Krems."
"Three and a half miles, Your Majesty."
"The French have abandoned the left bank?"
"According to the scouts, the last of them crossed on rafts during the night."
"Is there sufficient forage in Krems?"
"Forage has not been supplied to the extent—"
The Emperor cut him off.
"At what time was General Schmidt killed?"
"At seven o'clock, I believe."
"At seven o'clock? That is very sad, very sad!"

The Emperor thanked Prince Andrew and bowed. Prince Andrew withdrew and was immediately surrounded on all sides by courtiers. Everywhere he saw friendly faces and heard kind words. Yesterday's adjutant reproached him for not having stayed at the palace and offered him the use of his own house. The Minister of War came up to congratulate him on the Order of Maria Theresa, third class, which the Emperor was bestowing on him. The Empress's chamberlain invited him to see Her Majesty. The archduchess also wished to see him. He didn't know whom to respond to first and took a few seconds to collect his thoughts. Then the Russian ambassador took him by the shoulder, led him to the window, and began talking.

Contrary to Bilíbin's prediction, the news Prince Andrew had brought was received with joy. A thanksgiving service was arranged, Kutúzov was awarded the Grand Cross of Maria Theresa, and the entire army received decorations. Bolkónski was invited everywhere and had to spend the whole morning making calls on the leading Austrian dignitaries. Between four and five in the afternoon, having completed all his calls, he was walking back to Bilíbin's house, composing in his head a letter to his father about the battle and his visit to Brünn. At the door he found a carriage half-loaded with luggage. Franz, Bilíbin's servant, was struggling to drag a heavy trunk out through the front door.
Before returning to Bilíbin's, Prince Andrew had stopped at a bookshop to stock up on books for the campaign and had spent some time browsing.
"What's going on?" he asked.
"Oh, Your Excellency!" said Franz, wrestling the trunk toward the carriage. "We have to move on again. That scoundrel is at our heels!"
"What? What do you mean?" asked Prince Andrew.
Bilíbin came out to meet him. His usually calm face showed excitement.
"There now! You have to admit this is delightful," he said. "The Thabor Bridge affair, in Vienna... They've crossed it without firing a shot!"
Prince Andrew couldn't grasp what he meant.
"Where have you been that you don't know what every cab driver in town knows?"
"I've been at the archduchess's. I heard nothing there."
"And you didn't notice that everyone is packing up?"
"I didn't... What's this all about?" Prince Andrew asked impatiently.

"What's it about? The French have crossed the bridge that Auersperg was supposed to be defending, and the bridge was not blown up. So now Murat is racing down the road toward Brünn and will be here in a day or two."
"What? Here? But why didn't they blow up the bridge if it was mined?"
"That's exactly what I'd like to know. Nobody—not even Bonaparte himself—can explain it."
Bolkónski shrugged.
"But if the bridge has been crossed, it means the army is lost too. It'll be cut off," he said.

"That's precisely the situation," answered Bilíbin. "Listen. The French entered Vienna as I told you. Fine. The next day—which was yesterday—these gentlemen, the marshals Murat, Lannes, and Belliard, mount their horses and ride to the bridge. (Note that all three are Gascons.) 'Gentlemen,' says one of them, 'you know the Thabor Bridge is mined and double-mined, that there are serious fortifications at the bridgehead, and that fifteen thousand men have orders to blow it up and keep us from crossing. But it would please our sovereign Emperor Napoleon if we took this bridge, so let's go take it!' 'Yes, let's!' say the others. And off they go and take the bridge, cross it, and now their entire army is on this side of the Danube, marching toward us—toward you, and your supply lines."
"The marshals."
"Stop joking," said Prince Andrew, sadly and seriously. The news pained him, and yet at the same time he was pleased.

The moment he learned that the Russian army was in such a desperate position, it occurred to him that he was the one destined to lead it out of this crisis—that here was the Toulon that would lift him from the ranks of obscure officers and offer him his first step toward glory! As he listened to Bilíbin, he was already imagining how, upon reaching the army, he would present an opinion at the war council—the only plan that could save them—and how he alone would be entrusted with carrying it out.
"Stop the joking," he said.

"I'm not joking," Bilíbin went on. "Nothing could be more true or more tragic. These gentlemen ride onto the bridge alone, waving white handkerchiefs. They assure the officer on duty that they, the marshals, are on their way to negotiate with Prince Auersperg. He lets them into the bridgehead. They spin a thousand tall tales, saying the war is over, that Emperor Francis is arranging a meeting with Bonaparte, that they'd like to see Prince Auersperg, and so on. The officer sends for Auersperg. The gentlemen embrace the Austrian officers, crack jokes, sit on the cannons, and meanwhile a French battalion slips onto the bridge unnoticed, throws the detonation charges into the water, and reaches the fortifications. At last the lieutenant general himself appears—our dear Prince Auersperg von Mautern. 'Dearest enemy! Flower of the Austrian army! Hero of the Turkish wars! Hostilities are over, we can shake hands... Emperor Napoleon burns with impatience to make Prince Auersperg's acquaintance.' In short, these gentlemen—true Gascons—so bewildered him with their fine words, and he was so flattered by his sudden intimacy with the French marshals, and so dazzled by the sight of Murat's cloak and ostrich plumes, that he couldn't see what was right in front of him—and forgot he was supposed to be firing on the enemy!" Despite his animated delivery, Bilíbin didn't forget to pause after this bon mot to let it land. "The French battalion rushes the bridgehead, spikes the guns, and the bridge is taken! But the best part," he continued, his excitement subsiding under the pleasant momentum of his own story, "is that the sergeant in charge of the cannon—the one meant to give the signal to detonate the mines—seeing the French troops swarming onto the bridge, was about to fire. But Lannes grabbed his hand. The sergeant, who was clearly smarter than his general, went up to Auersperg and said: 'Prince, you're being deceived—these are the French!' Murat, seeing that all was lost if the sergeant was allowed to speak, turned to Auersperg with a look of feigned astonishment—a true Gascon—and said: 'I hardly recognize the world-famous Austrian discipline when you allow a subordinate to address you like that!' It was a stroke of genius. Prince Auersperg, feeling his authority challenged, ordered the sergeant arrested. Come on, you have to admit this Thabor Bridge business is magnificent! It's not exactly stupidity, and it's not exactly treachery either..."
"Bridgehead."
"That their fire gets into his eyes and he forgets that he ought to be firing at the enemy."
"It might be treachery," said Prince Andrew, vividly picturing the gray overcoats, the wounds, the gunpowder smoke, the sounds of battle, and the glory that awaited him.

"Not that either. That would put the court in too bad a light," replied Bilíbin. "It's not treachery, not villainy, not stupidity—it's just like Ulm... it's..." He seemed to be searching for the right expression. "It's... it's a case of Mack. We've been Macked," he concluded, feeling he had produced a fresh witticism that would make the rounds. His previously furrowed brow smoothed out with pleasure, and with a slight smile he began examining his nails.
"Where are you off to?" he said suddenly to Prince Andrew, who had risen and was heading toward his room.
"I'm leaving."
"Where?"
"To the army."
"But you were planning to stay two more days."
"Now I'm leaving at once."
And Prince Andrew, after giving instructions for his departure, went to his room.
"You know, my dear fellow," said Bilíbin, following him, "I've been thinking about you. Why are you going?"
And as proof of the finality of his opinion, all the wrinkles vanished from his face.
Prince Andrew looked at him questioningly and said nothing.
"Why are you going? I know you think it's your duty to gallop back to the army now that it's in danger. I understand. My dear fellow, it is heroism!"
"Not at all," said Prince Andrew.

"But as a philosopher, be a consistent one. Look at the other side of the question and you'll see that your duty is actually to take care of yourself. Leave the heroics to those who are no longer fit for anything else... You haven't been ordered to return, and you haven't been dismissed from here. So you can stay and go wherever our bad luck takes us. They say we're heading for Olmütz, and Olmütz is a perfectly decent town. You and I will travel comfortably in my carriage."
"Stop joking, Bilíbin," said Bolkónski.

"I'm speaking sincerely, as a friend! Think about it. Where are you going, and why, when you could stay here? You're facing one of two outcomes"—and the skin over his left temple puckered—"either you won't reach your regiment before peace is concluded, or you'll share in the defeat and disgrace of Kutúzov's entire army."
And Bilíbin smoothed his temple, feeling his dilemma was unanswerable.
"I can't argue about it," replied Prince Andrew coldly, though he was thinking: "I am going to save the army."
"My dear fellow, you are a hero!" said Bilíbin.
